bearings.paper_claim: Office-motivated legislators with log utility get transfers exactly proportional to their Bonacich centrality b = (I - beta*G)^-1 * 1 (Prop 1, eq 4, eq 17-18). With policy-motivated legislators the weights become modified Bonacich centralities depending on preferences and pivot probabilities (eq 15, Prop 2), which converge to the office-motivated allocation as the number of legislators grows (Prop 3). Reported network externality phi = 0.2088 (SE 0.0697) committee, 0.2165 (SE 0.0703) corrected, 0.0837 (SE 0.0262) alumni (Table 2).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.2.1 Prop 1; Sec 3.2.2 eq 15-16, Prop 2-3; Sec 4.1 eq 17-18; Sec 4.3 Table 2
bearings.system_side: kb_benchmark.py computes KB centrality on build_P(load_network()) with an out-walk matvec and delta = KB_DELTA (0.85) / spectral radius; stored radius 1.5019 and delta 0.56595 match. Docstring lines 2-5 say groups allocate IN PROPORTION TO KB centrality. The member desk reads kb_pct from the stored file.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Exact proportionality holds only under office motivation with log utility; the docstring overstates it for the general case. Under policy motivation the weights depend on preferences and pivot probabilities. The paper's empirical networks are undirected; the system kernel is directed. The delta-versus-phi comparison (0.85 of the bound versus phi 0.08-0.25) is not like-for-like: delta is a Katz decay on the kernel, phi is an SAR coefficient.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers in paper_claim match Table 2 and the Prop 1-3 text. The monotone-increasing statement holds for office-motivated legislators with log utility (abstract line 37); restrict it there and have the docstring say so. Theory social weights are normalized so each legislator's row sums to 1 (Sec 2); empirical W normalization is not confirmed by the text. Treat the delta-versus-phi comparison as suggestive only.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper deliberately does not use cosponsorship as the network, because cosponsorship is determined simultaneously with contributions (fn 30). Sample is U.S. House members in the 109th-113th Congresses (2004-2012 cycles); outcome is total PAC money in logs, trimmed at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Controls in Table 2: margin of victory -0.897, DW_ideology -1.077, chair +0.401.
bearings.system_side: kb_benchmark.py builds KB on build_P(load_network()); load_network reads congress_cosponsor_network_*.xlsx. The benchmark pools 533 members of both chambers (chamber field in data/engine/congestion.json). Raw Spearman with no controls. Stored values in kb_benchmark.json: optimizer all members 0.2468, CU money 0.1347, bank plus finserv 0.2304, legislative score 0.6535, each n=533; these match the rel. The top-decile unallocated list has 15 names, of which 6 are senators (Warren, Merkley, Kennedy, Gillibrand, Cruz, Scott), not 7.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A KB-versus-money correlation on the cosponsorship graph cannot test the equilibrium the paper derives, since cosponsorship is the endogenous network the paper excludes. The pooled two-chamber estimates need an UNSTRATIFIED label. Paper evidence is House-only, 2004-2012; the money window for the system file is not recorded.
bearings.verifier_note: Stored correlations, n values and the cosponsorship kernel path were verified against code and JSON. Senator count corrected from 7 to 6, using the House and Senate membership of the 15 names. Paper sample and fn 30 confirmed. Keep the rho values UNVERIFIED and UNSTRATIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Standard centralities do not explain PAC money (Table 4): committee degree 0.0004 (SE 0.0003), alumni degree -0.0018 (SE 0.0053), closeness 0.5902 (SE 0.4711), betweenness committee -4.9e-05 (SE 2.9e-05, significant at 10 percent only). R-squared is 0.148 in most Table 4 columns (0.149 in one). Likelihood-ratio tests reject phi = 0 for the Bonacich-type SAR term (11.127 committee, 9.615 alumni).
bearings.system_side: InfluenceScore = 0.60 normalized weighted out-degree + 0.25 betweenness + 0.15 eigenvector, confirmed at build_legislation_base_network.py 818-835. The AB13 retirement and the feed into the underdog lens Intrinsic composite were not located: a repo search found no AB13 reference in that file or elsewhere under fec.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper tests unweighted degree, closeness and betweenness on PAC money in House committee and alumni networks, 2004-2012. It does not test weighted out-degree on a cosponsorship graph, and it does not test legislative influence or bill passage. It supports only the narrow point that direction-blind degree and betweenness do not predict money; it is neutral on whether they measure influence.
bearings.verifier_note: Table 4 values verified. Corrected: betweenness is weakly significant in one column, and R-squared is 0.149 in one column, so 'explain nothing' and '0.148 in every specification' overstate. The link to InfluenceScore is an analogy, not a test; keep the relation weak.

bearings.paper_claim: Legislators value conformity with network peers, so a group pricing a legislator counts downstream effects through network walks (Bonacich multiplier), not only the legislator's own vote (Sec 2; Prop 1). The estimated externality is positive and significant: phi 0.2088 committee, 0.0837 alumni (Table 2).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 2 conformity utility and social weights; Sec 3.2.1 Prop 1; Sec 4.3 Table 2
bearings.system_side: flip_model.py pflip adds a one-hop peer term WP*nA/mAt where nA counts only neighbours in the pro camp, so a CU dollar to member m changes only m's own pflip. Neighbours change only when a conversion updates camp; optimize.py 136-144 then clears the cache with fm._cache.clear() and recomputes proximity.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's phi measures network autocorrelation in contributions, which may reflect correlated effects rather than vote conformity; the paper does not show that money to one member moves a peer's vote. The paper's equilibrium is two-sided; the system optimizes for one PAC, so the link is conceptual. Any continuous spillover term needs its own prereg look, not a calibration from this paper.
bearings.verifier_note: Code path and paper estimates verified. The code uses a discrete one-hop peer term, which the bearing correctly calls an extension suggestion. Keep weak.

related.why: Ardekani et al. apply Katz prestige centrality to New Zealand legislative networks (checked: Katz is the chosen measure; closeness and betweenness are described as less suited). B-P give an equilibrium reason for a Bonacich-type measure. PageRank comparison not checked.

Porter et al. analyse a network whose nodes are committees, linked by common membership (checked in text). B-P build member-level ties from shared committees. Same underlying data, different network object; the rel description of a member co-membership network is corrected here.

Sotoudeh et al. build a cosponsorship-based influence measure and report it is more indicative of bill passage than off-the-shelf centralities (checked in abstract). They do not find cosponsorship centrality weak. B-P avoid cosponsorship as endogenous to money. Together: cosponsorship networks are contested inputs, not a validated influence signal.
Title matches: co-voting network centrality as a measure of political influence (checked; the text file is an online appendix of about 11,000 characters, so the link is verified at title level only).

Checked: budget-constrained influence over networked voters with an opposing controller (shadowing and shielding), so the competing-budgeted-actors framing holds. Calling it the dynamic counterpart of B-P is a characterization, kept as is.

Bonica recovers ideology for candidates and contributors from campaign contributions (checked in abstract). The claim that PACs allocate by competitiveness was not checked in the text; the link is kept as complements on the ideology side only.

summary_issues: Overstatement: 'Degree, closeness and betweenness explain nothing'. Betweenness is weakly significant in the committee column (-4.9e-05, 10 percent level).
R-squared: 'R^2 stays at 0.148' holds for most Table 4 columns; one column reports 0.149.
Count error: 'Seven of the 15 top-decile unallocated members are senators'. The list has six senators: Warren, Merkley, Kennedy, Gillibrand, Cruz, Scott.
Scope of monotonicity: 'transfers are a monotonically increasing function of Bonacich centrality' is stated generally; the paper's abstract limits it to office-motivated legislators.
Comparison: 'where the paper estimates a weaker spillover of about 0.08 to 0.25'. phi is an SAR coefficient on a different scale from the Katz delta, so 'weaker' is not a like-for-like comparison.

Normalization: 'The garbled text layer does not confirm' row normalization. The theory line says social weights are normalized so each legislator's row sums to 1; empirical W normalization remains unconfirmed.
The 'modest support' for keeping InfluenceScore out of the rank rests on unweighted degree and betweenness tested on PAC money; InfluenceScore itself was not tested. Analogy only.
Related-link descriptions for Porter (committee-node network) and Sotoudeh (their own influence measure beats centralities; not weak cosponsorship centrality) were corrected in related.
paul_alignment was not verified against Paul's annotation document; the B-P entry has no annotation text, and the claims about Paul's cosponsorship plans and Ardekani highlights were not checked.
Not located in code: the AB13 retirement and the underdog lens Intrinsic composite feed for InfluenceScore.

Coverage limits: the text layer garbles Greek symbols and some equations; Table A.1, the online appendix and figures are not in the text file. The ext and rel overrides were absent, so the item JSON ext and rel fields were used.
